headline: High: OpenHands can write and browse while Plane ingests files and exposes issue/task data, creating default-path leakage and cascading-error risks; prompt injection is lower because no shared channel is documented.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenHands can use MCP, browsers, and filesystem writes, while Plane accepts file uploads and hyperlinks. No shared channel is documented, so direct injection is not proven; however, if the operator bridges them by copying Plane content into OpenHands or via a shared mounted volume, prompt injection becomes plausible. Plane itself is not shown parsing instructions.
conditions: IF Plane content is copied into OpenHands prompts or MCP inputs, injected instructions can steer tool use.
IF both agents share a mounted volume containing untrusted Plane exports, OpenHands may treat them as instructions.
mitigations: Keep Plane exports out of OpenHands prompts.
Disable shared-volume handoff for untrusted files.
Use a read-only staging folder for any copied artifacts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: OpenHands reads files in its runtime sandbox and can send data to a configured model provider; Plane stores issues, tasks, notes, files, and images. If the same workspace or mounted volume is shared, sensitive Plane data can flow into OpenHands and then to a third-party backend. Plane's own egress is broad, so the pair can leak work products in default-ish setups.
conditions: IF Plane files or notes are mounted into OpenHands's runtime, OpenHands can read them.
IF OpenHands is configured with an external model provider, copied Plane content may leave the local environment.
mitigations: Do not mount Plane data into OpenHands unless necessary.
Use a local-only model provider for OpenHands.
Redact sensitive issue attachments before transfer.
Separate credentials and API keys between the two systems.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenHands can write the filesystem and modify git state; Plane cannot write the filesystem but can still receive uploads and broad network traffic. The main conflict is not direct write-write collision, but shared mutable resources via mounted volumes or external services can still race or overwrite artifacts. Uncertainty remains because Plane's deployment mode is not fully specified.
conditions: IF Plane is deployed against the same mounted directory that OpenHands edits, file races can occur.
IF both systems act on the same external ticket or artifact without locking, last-writer-wins conflicts can occur.
mitigations: Avoid concurrent edits to the same git branch.
Use explicit locking or a single-writer workflow.
Pause one agent before the other mutates shared artifacts.

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenHands can generate code, files, and browser-derived content; Plane stores issues, tasks, and notes that may be treated as authoritative work items. If Plane ingests OpenHands output without verification, errors can cascade into task tracking or scheduling decisions. Plane's lack of browser/tooling reduces direct action risk, but not propagation risk.
conditions: IF Plane imports OpenHands-generated text into issues or tasks without review, incorrect facts can propagate.
IF OpenHands writes summaries that Plane uses as source-of-truth, downstream work items may be wrong.
mitigations: Require human review before creating Plane issues from OpenHands output.
Add a verification checklist for any imported summary.
Keep source links alongside derived notes.

E_compliance.rationale: OpenHands handles model-provider API keys and files in a Docker runtime; Plane stores issues, tasks, files, images, and notes and exposes email/forum/security contact surfaces. The profiles do not specify residency or certifications, so compliance mismatch cannot be ruled out. Because uncertainty escalates and both touch potentially sensitive work data, medium is the safest supported level.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in Plane and then copied into OpenHands, residency or retention obligations may be implicated.
IF either deployment routes data to a region or vendor not approved for that data class, compliance gaps arise.
mitigations: Classify data before moving it between systems.
Confirm retention settings in both deployments.
Avoid placing regulated data in either system unless approved.
Document the data flow and responsible owner.
